name: DotCurio
tagline: A curated directory with listing pages, side by side comparison and search.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The software here is a solved problem: a list of entries, filter and sort, a detail page, a compare view, full text search. An agent will hand you all of that in an afternoon with static files and client side search, and it will be fast because your dataset is small. What it will not hand you is the part that makes a directory worth opening, which is a person deciding what gets in and what gets cut. Build it for yourself and you get a clean personal reference; build it to replace someone else's directory and you have signed up for permanent unpaid editorial work. The build is a weekend at most, the curation is forever.
coreLoopDIY: Generates a static, searchable directory site from Markdown entry files, with filters, detail pages and a two or three way compare table.
requirements: Your own entry data, written as Markdown or pasted from a spreadsheet
Somewhere static to host it if you want it public
whatYouLose: The curation itself: someone else's taste, research hours and judgment on what is worth listing
New and updated entries arriving without you doing anything
Whatever structured fields the maintainer has already normalized across every listing
Discoverability: a public directory gets found, your local one does not
Small polish you will not bother with, like OG images per entry and keyboard driven search
moatNotes: The dataset is the product. The code around it is scaffolding, and scaffolding is exactly what coding agents are good at.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because nobody wants to maintain a directory, they want to consult one. Paying means the entries are already researched, the fields are already comparable, and new items show up without you auditing a category at 1am. A self built clone is honest about that trade: you own the shape of the data and lose the stream of it. If the specific niche matters to your work and the curation is actually good, the subscription is cheaper than your evenings.
notes: The directory engine is a weekend; the directory is not.
prompt:
Build a static, searchable curated directory site in an empty folder.

Stack, non negotiable: Astro 4 with content collections, TypeScript, Tailwind for styling, FlexSearch for client side search. No database, no backend, no auth, no analytics, no telemetry. Everything builds to static HTML.

Data model: a content collection called `entries`, one Markdown file per item in `src/content/entries/`. Frontmatter schema, validated with zod: title, slug, url, oneLiner, category (string), tags (string array), price (number or null), priceNote (string or null), pros (string array), cons (string array), rating (1 to 5 or null), addedOn (date), updatedOn (date or null). Markdown body is the long form take.

Pages to generate:
1. `/` listing page: card grid of all entries, client side filter by category and tag, sort by addedOn, title or rating, and a search box wired to FlexSearch over title, oneLiner, tags and body text. Filters live in the URL query string so views are shareable.
2. `/entry/[slug]` detail page: full frontmatter rendered as a spec table, pros and cons side by side, rendered Markdown body, outbound link with rel="noopener".
3. `/compare?ids=a,b,c` compare view: up to three entries in one table, one row per frontmatter field, visually mark rows where values differ. Pick entries via checkboxes on the listing page.
4. `/categories/[category]` for each distinct category value.

Also generate: sitemap.xml, RSS feed of entries sorted by addedOn, and a per entry OG image using Astro's satori or a simple SVG template.

Seed with eight realistic example entries across three categories so every page and the diff highlighting are visibly working.

Include an `npm run new-entry` script that scaffolds a Markdown file with empty frontmatter.

Out of scope, do not build: user accounts, submission forms, comments, an admin UI, a CMS, any paid API. If anything later needs a key, read it from .env via import.meta.env and commit a .env.example only.

Finish with a README covering: how to add an entry, how to deploy the static output, and a one line note that the hard part of a directory is the entries, not this code.
